gist: Inflation means the same money buys less: US prices roughly doubled since 2000.
The 2021-22 spike had several causes stacked together: money and demand, supply chains, energy and some company pricing.
Inflation quietly moves buying power between shoppers, savers, workers, borrowers and governments.

books.title: How The Boring Company Digs
books.blurb: Wren's field journal tests one mile of tunnel: why subways cost $100 million to $1 billion+ a mile, how a tunnel boring machine digs, Prufrock's tricks, how the Vegas Loop works, what a mile costs from Madrid to New York, and what Boring promised vs delivered.
gist: Tunnels are slow and costly: a standard TBM digs a mile in 8 to 12 weeks, and big-city lines cost $100 million to $1 billion+ a mile, mostly in stations.
Boring shrinks the tunnel to 12 ft and builds its own Prufrock machines; the first Vegas Loop cost about $60 million a route mile, and Prufrock digs about a mile a month against a mile-a-week goal.
The Vegas Loop has 14 stations and 4 million+ riders, but cars at about 35 mph carry far fewer people than trains, several city projects were dropped, and safety and oversight questions remain.
books.tagline: Smaller tunnels, no pits, no stopping. Does it scale?

recap: Problem: big tunnels cost $100 million to $1 billion+ a mile and dig slower than a snail.
How: a TBM cuts, balances, pushes and lines; Prufrock aims to skip pits and stops, and digs about a mile a month vs a mile-a-week goal.
Different: about $60 million a route mile for the first Vegas Loop vs $130 million (Madrid) to $4.4 billion (New York), but far lower capacity.
Next: Paradise Road extension, Nashville and Dubai; the 90,000-an-hour goal is unproven.
